item.description: A Science cover paper claims pigeons navigate using liver macrophages on cloudy days; three magnetoreception veterans countered with calculations showing thermal noise swamps magnetic signals by 30-fold at body temperature—rendering the mechanism physically untenable.
item.content:encoded:
A Science cover paper claims pigeons navigate using liver macrophages on cloudy days; three magnetoreception veterans countered with calculations showing thermal noise swamps magnetic signals by 30-fold at body temperature—rendering the mechanism physically untenable.

If you want to watch a cover paper get methodically dismantled by peers within two months of publication, this episode presents the experiments and calculations from both debate sides with high density.

20:12 Authorization to spend is not the same as getting the money
Congress's authorization only sets an agency's mandate and spending caps; it does not constitute actual disbursement. Real funding requires separate appropriations legislation. The Chips and Science Act exemplifies this: it provided genuine appropriations for semiconductors but merely authorized expansion of federal research projects without real funding attached. Understanding this distinction explains why headlines like "Congress approved billions in research funding" are often overstated.

22:24 White House memos seek political appointees' say in research funding allocation
Historically, federal agencies' decisions on which research teams receive funding came from peer review by scientists and program officers, with Congress controlling only broad budget direction. Before this midterm cycle, Trump administration memos asked the Office of Management and Budget to shift allocation authority toward political appointees over individual projects instead of expert scientists—viewed as challenging both congressional fiscal authority and agency autonomy.

51:57 The iron-rich beak cells scientists thought were neurons are actually macrophages
The classic 1960s-70s hypothesis that pigeons sensed magnetic fields via magnetite particles in their beaks like compasses was widely accepted until 2012. David Keays's team used staining techniques to demonstrate these iron-rich cells were not neurons but macrophages—immune system scavengers that clear dead red blood cells and accumulate iron—lacking the capacity to rapidly transmit sensory signals to the brain. The magnetite hypothesis was thereby overturned.

54:30 Quantum-entangled electron pairs might let birds see magnetic fields
The radical pair hypothesis proposes that blue light photons excite electrons in retinal cryptochrome proteins, generating entangled electron pairs in singlet or triplet states that interact differently with Earth's magnetic field, eventually creating signals distinguishing magnetic direction. Yet the mechanism depends on blue light and cannot explain pigeons navigating in complete darkness, nor does it account for naturally blind bats also possessing magnetoreception.

1:07:24 Kill liver macrophages, and pigeons lose their way on cloudy days
The Science cover paper found iron-rich liver macrophages displaying superparamagnetism at low temperatures, with electron microscopy revealing them pressed against neurons connecting to the vagus nerve. When researchers selectively killed macrophages using liposomal clodronate, they fitted 34 pigeons with GPS trackers and released them along a 19-kilometer route: on clear days both groups navigated home normally; on cloudy days with killed macrophages, pigeons became completely disoriented with scattered paths, while cloudy-day birds with intact macrophages still found their way accurately.

1:21:49 At body temperature, thermal noise drowns the magnetic signal by 30-fold
Leading magnetoreception experts including Hora and Moritzson countered: the magnetic component in ferritin is antiferromagnetic magnetite with minuscule magnetic moment. Calculations show its interaction energy under Earth's field strength at avian body temperature (300K) is 30 times smaller than thermal noise—molecules vibrate too violently to sense such weak force. Superparamagnetism measured in the paper only holds below 12K, a critical temperature gap from warm-blooded pigeons.

1:25:00 The magnetic field from that 1974 experiment never reached the liver
Magnetoreception pioneers Charles Walcott and Joseph Kirschvnik recalculated their own 1974 Helmholtz coil experiment with the device mounted on pigeon heads: if the coil's interfering field were to affect the distant abdominal liver, the leaked field strength at the liver would change only by 1.4%—far too small to explain the birds' complete loss of directional sense in that experiment. This contradicts the liver hypothesis against those classic results.

1:28:06 Macrophages move around; how can a moving compass ever work
A neurobiological counter-argument notes that an effective car compass must be fixed to the vehicle to consistently indicate direction. But macrophages' function is to roam the body seeking debris to engulf—position and orientation constantly shift. For the brain to synthesize a reliable magnetic direction from thousands of moving "mini compasses" each oriented differently requires unrealistic computational overhead, making liver macrophages as direct navigation sensors implausible.

item.title: Ramp Paused Hiring for a Quarter to Force AI Mastery
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-18-ycsp-ramp-内部不招人一个季度-只为逼团队学会用-ai/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-18-ycsp-ramp-内部不招人一个季度-只为逼团队学会用-ai/
item.description: Ramp discovered engineers' productivity increased 100x with AI, but salespeople and designers couldn't keep up and would drag down the organization, so they froze hiring for an entire quarter and forced everyone to make AI a core competency rather than an ancillary skill.
item.content:encoded:
Ramp discovered engineers' productivity increased 100x with AI, but salespeople and designers couldn't keep up and would drag down the organization, so they froze hiring for an entire quarter and forced everyone to make AI a core competency rather than an ancillary skill.

Ramp's co-CEO explains how a $6 billion company embeds AI into financial workflows, internal tools, and organizational structure—not abstract concepts, but specific mechanisms and numbers that make this worth listening to in full.

22:01 1% of users consumed 80% of tokens, structural friction emerged
A few engineers saw productivity surge to its extreme with AI—not exaggerating, 100x—while designers, product managers and other roles couldn't keep up. This destroyed the traditional ratio of one product manager and one designer per six to eight engineers. Engineers began outpacing the rest of the company, creating structural friction within the organization.

23:05 Pausing hiring for a quarter forces teams to truly master AI
Eric noticed a counterintuitive correlation: the more people used AI, the less they needed to hire; the less people used AI, the greater the hiring need. So earlier this year, while business was growing over 100%, Ramp decided not to hire for an entire quarter. The reason wasn't just that hiring is time-consuming—more importantly, they didn't want AI learning to consume only 5% of employees' time, but to make it a core competency.

24:09 The real barrier for large companies to adopt AI is terminal access
Small companies can get everyone on AI easily, but at big companies when sales wants to use Claude Code, they first need to open a terminal, install packages, then request access to Databricks, Snowflake, Slack, Stripe—and often get stuck right there. Eric believes most people experience AI like ‘passing notes through a wall’ rather than the way top engineers do it: AI connected directly to systems with permissions, integrated into the team.

32:45 AI expense approval makes purely ceremonial gatekeeper positions redundant
Companies must have someone review every expense for compliance reasons—a requirement stemming from Sarbanes-Oxley—but most approvers actually don't care about policies and either rubber-stamp everything or go through motions, often getting it wrong. Ramp built a policy agent that can automatically approve, reject, or flag incomplete policies with 99% accuracy, and every manual override teaches the system, even retroactively refining the policies themselves.

40:06 Coase's theorem debate: AI converges to one firm or enables thousands
There are two extreme views on how AI reshapes firm size. One is ‘doomsday’: some lab wins everything, the optimal number of companies approaches one. The other: AI enables hyper-specialization, letting thousands of companies each become billion-dollar champions in narrow verticals. Eric explicitly backs the second view and says Ramp is ‘betting’ on it.

41:06 Jevons paradox broke for the first time in the past two months
When intelligence got 10% cheaper, usage would grow faster than price fell—like how cheaper railways increased transport demand. This held for AI too. But Eric directly points out it broke in the past two months: model capabilities keep climbing, but society's capacity to digest that capability has hit a ceiling. It may be a local maximum, not necessarily permanent.

44:33 Non-engineer pull requests jumped from zero to 7,000 in a single quarter
Ramp had 7,000 pull requests created by non-engineers in Q2, while two years ago the number was basically zero—no one would let people who hadn't learned git submit code. Most came from the customer experience team. They used to file bugs with product managers for scheduling, wait on designers, wait on engineers, and get fixes two months later. Now they can fix it themselves and ship the same day.

48:22 System-of-record companies that don't become AI harnesses will die
Gary brought up a slightly controversial tweet he'd posted: ‘Either die as a system-of-record company or live long enough to become an AI harness.’ Eric explicitly agreed and said Ramp doesn't consider itself fintech but a productivity company, where the core question is always ‘How do you make your money and time go further?’

item.title: In court, she asked not for mercy but to be judged with her comrades
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-18-stuffmissed-审判席上她不求宽恕-只要求与同志们一起受罚/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-18-stuffmissed-审判席上她不求宽恕-只要求与同志们一起受罚/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: The French government thought exile and imprisonment would tame her; instead, Louise Michel refused to defend herself in court, publicly admitted to every act in the Paris Commune, and demanded a death sentence.
item.content:encoded:
The French government thought exile and imprisonment would tame her; instead, Louise Michel refused to defend herself in court, publicly admitted to every act in the Paris Commune, and demanded a death sentence.

A biographical episode dense with information from her trial testimony and exile, manageable in a single commute.

3:02 Born outside marriage, she had access to education that most rural girls lacked
Her parents never married, and she was raised by her grandparents in what locals called ‘the grave’—a crumbling castle. This marginal but relatively affluent position gave her something rare for a rural girl of her era: access to books, neighborhood reading groups, and education. This would later fuel her challenge to educational inequality between men and women.

8:07 At twelve, she refused marriage and never reconsidered
When she was twelve or thirteen, two adult men proposed to her grandfather. Unusually, he let her decide. She shamed the first suitor with a quote from Molière, and dismissed the second more directly. This was not teenage rebellion—her memoirs state clearly that she rejected marriage for life, seeing it as fundamentally a torment inflicted on women.

16:20 She aimed to erase the line between boys' education and girls' education
From the start of her teaching career, Michel worked to eliminate the difference between how boys and girls were educated. She observed that schools filled girls with ‘a pile of drivel propping up infantile logic’ while forcing boys to swallow ‘science pill by pill’—both outcomes she found absurd. This was not abstract principle: her school taught boys and girls together and ran night classes to stay open.

23:23 The Paris Commune gave her a chance to implement her program
When the Commune was established, Michel's demands were specific, not abstract: equal education for girls and boys, coordination between schools and families, career paths for young women after graduation, inclusion of disabled children in regular classes, equal pay for male and female teachers, and basic rights to food and shelter for all. Her anarchism was not hollow destruction; it was a complete social welfare platform.

27:30 At trial, she asked the court to sentence her to death
The Versailles military court charged her with attempting to overthrow the government, inciting civil war, bearing arms in military dress, forging documents, and participating in executions of hostages. Michel admitted every charge, asked for no mercy, confessed to setting fires to block the Versailles army, and demanded the death penalty. The court sentenced her to exile in New Caledonia instead.

30:34 In exile, she turned her fight against the colonizers
Exiled to New Caledonia in the South Pacific, Michel aligned herself with the Kanak indigenous people against French colonizers, openly urging them to take up arms. She also taught them French so they could negotiate with the colonists themselves. Her anarchism did not fade in exile; it found new ground.

32:36 Bread, work, or bullets: the 1883 uprising
In 1883, she organized unemployed Parisians in a demonstration that turned into a riot. Protesters chanted ‘Bread, work, or bullets’—a warning that failure to address jobs and hunger would bring violence. She reportedly carried a black flag, which would later become anarchism's symbol, though her role in hoisting it remains unconfirmed. After weeks in hiding, she turned herself in for trial.

37:44 The state tried to prove she was mad rather than try her again
When arrested again in 1890, the authorities did not proceed with trial. Instead they attempted to have her declared mentally ill so they could institutionalize her. After her release, she fled to London, where she spent five years giving lectures, running an anarchist school, and organizing, until 1895 when she returned to Paris, the city she loved.

item.title: AI Builds You a ‘Second Self’ That Even the Founder Can't See
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-18-a16z-ai给你建一个-第二人格-连创始人都看不到你的那份/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-18-a16z-ai给你建一个-第二人格-连创始人都看不到你的那份/
item.description: First Person Labs separates data from inference: models run locally or in confidential computing, the company itself cannot prove it can see your content, trust rests on hardware not promises.
item.content:encoded:
First Person Labs separates data from inference: models run locally or in confidential computing, the company itself cannot prove it can see your content, trust rests on hardware not promises.

This episode covers the system architecture and privacy design of personal AI assistant ‘Second’, technically oriented—skip the product intro at the beginning, the real information points are in the middle and later sections on confidential computing and cost modeling.

2:02 Preferences sync in seconds, no need to re-brief the agent
Ken Liu's example: flight-seat preference, early-airport time, first-class interest—these things used to need re-explaining every time you switched to a new tool (like from GrokBot to Codex). Second's approach is to continuously build a model of a person's preferences, relationships, and intentions in the background; when users switch to any agent, this model can sync ‘in seconds’ without multiple follow-up questions. Ken mentioned switching to OpenAI's newly-released Codex model, where work context accumulated in Second was directly usable.

5:08 Your computer already knows what you're doing—no one's just been analyzing it
Ken Liu points out that systems already have an endless stream of events at the system level: app switches, page dwell time, typing speed, Wi-Fi connection state—data already exposed by Apple, Microsoft, and Linux systems themselves. First Person Labs does what a 24/7 agent does: analyze this stream layer by layer, inferring ‘checking messages’ from a single keystroke, and ‘doing research’ or ‘writing a document’ from cross-app switching, building a layered understanding of what a person is doing. Ken's conclusion: people severely underestimate how much computers already know.

7:11 Real productivity isn't answering messages—it's connecting the dots
Ken Liu divides personal AI output into two layers: ‘reactive’ productivity just responds to single events, like notifying when an email arrives—this layer is easy and already overabundant. The harder part is ‘reflective’ productivity—understanding across months and multiple events, like remembering goals stated months ago, spotting how recent behavior pushes toward that goal, combined with known preferences for judgment. He believes the future direction of personal computing isn't users constantly asking questions, but systems actively deciding when to intervene: ‘people still have to speak up and ask now, but that's really the problem—you shouldn't have to constantly ask a super-intelligent agent’.

11:21 Trust is built on hardware, not company promises
Ken Liu separates AI into two things: data and inference. Users can bring their own tokens and hand their data to inference providers of their own choosing, with no need to trust First Person Labs at all. A further step is ‘confidential inference’—putting models inside GPUs that support confidential computing, where after enabling a hardware switch you can cryptographically prove ‘only this model runs inside, no one can see in’. The object of trust shifts from company to Nvidia hardware. This is completely different from the common ‘zero data retention’ promise: the latter is just a policy-level guarantee from the company (even if legally binding); the former is a verifiable technical fact.

14:23 Data stays entirely local, just like a password vault
Second offers two storage approaches. One called Second Local keeps data only on the user's machine, leaving only when the user picks a reasoning service—like locking a password vault locally instead of uploading to Dropbox. The other is cloud backup, following the iCloud or password-manager approach: encrypt locally then upload, decryption only happens when users actively operate (briefly existing in memory) or the entire storage environment sits inside a container that can be remotely verified like confidential inference. The two paths together form ‘local encryption → cloud upload → decryption only inside a trusted container’.

18:25 Analyzing one person 24/7 costs this much per day
Ken Liu did the math on stage: assuming an agent running 24 hours, 60 tokens per second, and to handle the volume you need 10 such agents running simultaneously, using Opus pricing this comes to about 1000 dollars per day. Switch to DeepSeek Flash at the same volume and it's only about 60 dollars per day. He believes this cost will drop rapidly as new models replace each other—since First Person Labs was founded, token prices have dropped over 50%. This is why Second now feels aimed at ‘busy professionals’ willing to pay for deep personal context rather than everyone.

20:26 Screenshot plus ‘fix’ saves you from explaining context
Ken Liu shared the most surprising use case in development: because Second has such strong memory of ‘what we're doing’, users no longer need to brief a coding agent about background—just screenshot and say ‘fix’, the agent knows what to change. He also mentioned ‘context continuity’: browsing through on a notebook then closing, switching to a phone, the same context continues on the phone, even continuing to write the same email on mobile.

30:37 Company deliberately limits interaction to text and API only
Responding to ‘you're doing both foundational secure infrastructure and delightful user experience—isn't that schizophrenia?’, Ken Liu admits the team once pushed hard on interaction design, then discovered the difficulty was immense—‘delightful experience’ has too many details to polish. So the company's decision was to narrow the interfaces it exposes: ‘only text, only API, nothing else’, leaving the real work of building personalized interfaces and applications to users and developers, while they themselves first solidify the bottom layer: ‘everyone will eventually need a Second’.

item.title: GTA6 Burned Billions, but Rockstar Says That's an Outlier, Not the Industry Blueprint
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-18-oddlots-gta6烧掉十几亿美元-但制作人说这是个例-不是行业范本/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-18-oddlots-gta6烧掉十几亿美元-但制作人说这是个例-不是行业范本/
item.description: Rockstar can spend billions because GTA's track record makes success certain, while other studios are cutting budgets because sales haven't kept pace with rising costs—GTA6's formula can't be replicated.
item.content:encoded:
Rockstar can spend billions because GTA's track record makes success certain, while other studios are cutting budgets because sales haven't kept pace with rising costs—GTA6's formula can't be replicated.

To understand how a game can take 8 years and cost billions while guaranteeing profit, and why only Rockstar can pull off this strategy; the mid-section on game design and AI's competition for computing power is especially rich.

9:10 Cosmetics in a Game Outearns the Game Itself
GTA Online became a money machine after GTA V's release; microtransactions on clothing, weapons, and similar items generate roughly $500 million yearly. For Take-Two, in-game spending accounts for about 80% of company revenue—far more than game sales. This explains why Rockstar wasn't rushing a sequel: as long as GTA Online kept printing cash, the opportunity cost of delay shrank.

11:19 Making This Game Doubled the Studio's Headcount
Red Dead Redemption 2 ended with 2,400 Rockstar employees; GTA6 required 4,700. This isn't just GTA6's story—it's an industry trend: games have evolved from 2-3 years and $20 million budgets to 7-8 years and costs in the hundreds of millions, possibly exceeding $1 billion.

16:26 Two Characters Playing Together Stretched Development
When the player controls Jason or Lucia, the other character performs believable responses automatically—walking to the car door and sitting down when entering a vehicle, moving to a stationary bike in the next room to exercise. This system—where every character the player doesn't control must behave like a real person—required programming, art, and QA working in lockstep. Jason Schreier emphasizes it's far less predictable than ordinary software, and was a concrete reason development stretched.

21:30 Total Realism Became Tedium, So Rockstar Abandoned It
In Red Dead Redemption 2, hunting deer required shooting, skinning, and tying the carcass to your horse—a grueling sequence many players loved for its immersion. For GTA6, the team ultimately chose a faster, more arcade-like pace instead of piling on tedious realistic mechanics, trading immersive systems for snappy GTA-style gameplay.

31:48 The Pandemic Closed the Motion Capture Stage, and Killed the Schedule
Extensive cutscenes and dialogue relied on actors in motion-capture studios; all such studios closed during the pandemic, halting production—a documented source of delay in the 8-year development cycle. Whether the expensive production pipeline and team chemistry now built will actually speed up the next game is uncertain, Schreier says; the industry has never been here before.

36:58 GTA6's Gameplay Trailer Outdraws a De Niro Film
Rockstar premiered a half-hour GTA6 gameplay trailer on Netflix this summer; that week, the most-watched content on the platform wasn't a film or series—it was the game trailer, outperforming Robert De Niro's new release. PlayStation and Xbox both reported that GTA6 shattered their respective preorder records; estimates put preorders above 10 million.

42:06 AI Drained GPU Stocks, and Console Prices Rose for the First Time
AI chip demand pushed GPU prices higher; PC gamers paid double or triple for high-end cards and still couldn't find them in stock. Consoles, though not customizable, also faced their first-ever price increases due to supply constraints: PS5 launched at $500 and the base model now costs $650. Industry insiders worry next-generation consoles could exceed $1,000.

43:09 Take-Two's CEO: Only Rockstar Earns Unlimited Budget
Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick joked about Rockstar's spending with a wedding metaphor: he told his son the wedding budget had no limit, and his son actually overran it. The joke conceals a serious judgment—GTA's brand power makes Rockstar nearly the only studio that can guarantee money spent will return profit. Most other game companies are figuring out how to cut budgets, because sales haven't kept pace with rising costs.

item.title: The Ming opened trade when military victory failed—and war vanished
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-18-cn27f438-明朝打不过蒙古就开放互市-战争立刻消失了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-18-cn27f438-明朝打不过蒙古就开放互市-战争立刻消失了/
item.description: After decades of fighting pirates and Mongols to exhaustion, opening trade under Longqing ended the conflicts, revealing that trade isn't zero-sum—instead, rules often emerge from the contact surface between exhausted opponents.
item.content:encoded:
After decades of fighting pirates and Mongols to exhaustion, opening trade under Longqing ended the conflicts, revealing that trade isn't zero-sum—instead, rules often emerge from the contact surface between exhausted opponents.

Three historical periods show how rules emerge from contact—Ming border trade, Shanghai's opening, and modern globalization. The common thread—that order grows from conflict surfaces—suits anyone studying institutional change.

2:32 Yangyang backpacks on African market stalls reveal China's scale
Shi Zhan saw backpacks with the Yangyang (喜羊羊) cartoon character on a roadside stall in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania—cheaply made yet shipped thousands of miles from Yiwu or Dongguan because Chinese scale made it cheaper than local production. This moment crystallized his understanding of China's sheer size and launched his decades-long inquiry: how did this scale form, and can it endure?

8:09 Open trade in military stalemate and you end conflict
For 40 years the Jiajing era endured waves from south (pirates) and north (Mongols). The dynasty fought itself to exhaustion without pacifying either threat. The Mongols' actual demand was straightforward: permission to trade. Jiajing refused. His successor Longqing pivoted: he lifted the maritime ban in the southeast (centered in Zhangzhou) and opened Ming-Mongol trade. War stopped.

13:09 Trade is positive-sum, war is zero-sum
Conflict between farming and pastoral societies at borders is fundamentally a clash of different peoples. War tends toward stalemate—neither side wins, both bleed out. That's zero-sum or worse. Trade is a plus game: both gain. This wasn't moral idealism but fiscal reality: endless warfare bankrupted the state, forcing pragmatism.

14:26 Stranger societies run on contracts, not on personal trust
Fei Xiaotong described rural China as ordered by kinship and locality—a "differential order" where relationships trump formal rules. Shanghai, a port city of migrants (Ningbo bankers, Jiangbei natives, Subei natives), had no shared informal defaults. Each group's rules contradicted the others'. It switched to impersonal rules: contracts, deeds, documents. These address transactions, not persons. They scale faster and wider—why Shanghai entered modernity earlier.

18:13 New treaty port tariffs prevented dynasty collapse during rebellion
Every dynasty collapsed when rebels seized the fiscal heartland. The Qing alone escaped: the Taiping Rebellion conquered the Yangtze valley and the empire's financial core. Yet the Qing survived. Why? Shanghai's opening brought a fiscal source history had never seen: tariffs on seaborne trade, plus inland transit taxes (likin). The latter also indirectly funded Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang's armies.

22:18 Shanghai once rejected outsiders with fierce local pride
Liu Qing arrived as a university student in 1978. Speaking anything but fluent Shanghainese meant different treatment from bus conductors and bookstore clerks in daily transactions. Even buying a seven-fen ticket required the accent. He traces this to the 1960s-70s when Shanghai only exported people (to broadcast stations and the countryside) while blocking incomers, breeding intense localism.

25:20 Order and freedom contradict; conflict changes the rules
People need both: rules provide stability, belonging, community. But rules also constrain freedom, novelty, risk. These wants clash. So people constantly break rules to claim freedom; failure drives retreat to order. How do rules change? Friction: new things press against old rules. This friction is China's engine of institutional change because geographic and cultural diversity means constant collision and renewal.

28:21 Shanghai proved Musk's impossible dream could actually work
Musk is not a manager carving a niche in an existing market. He imagined a totally new path for humanity, with EVs as a step. Model S launched in 2018 but couldn't scale. By 2019 Shanghai's Gigafactory rose in 11 months and began production. Shanghai soon accounted for over half global Tesla output and even greater profit share. Only then did capital markets believe his vision was real. His valuation took off.

item.title: ‘Invasive species are doing their own work’: Indigenous ecological knowledge doesn't use a good-bad binary
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-18-ologies-入侵物种也在-干自己的活-原住民生态知识不用好坏二分法/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-18-ologies-入侵物种也在-干自己的活-原住民生态知识不用好坏二分法/
item.description: Species commonly labeled ‘invasive’—like European honeybees and Asian ladybugs—are viewed in indigenous ecological knowledge as fulfilling their own ecological roles, not as black-and-white enemies.
item.content:encoded:
Species commonly labeled ‘invasive’—like European honeybees and Asian ladybugs—are viewed in indigenous ecological knowledge as fulfilling their own ecological roles, not as black-and-white enemies.

The densest information comes in the middle and latter sections, particularly worth hearing for the distinction between cultural fire and government-controlled burns, and the position of indigenous scientists in academia.

8:05 Honeybees don't come native or invasive—only working or not
The Oneida Nation's own orchards specifically borrow European honeybees from Florida farms for pollination; these bees are not native to North America, yet they're crucial labor for increasing yields. Cheyenne says indigenous languages often lack the word ‘invasive species’, instead using a framework where every species has work to do, and European honeybees are no exception. This directly contrasts with mainstream conservation discourse's default stance that ‘invasive = must eliminate’.

9:11 Endangered bumblebees are rebounding in indigenous-managed reserves
According to data from the Xerxes Society for Invertebrate Conservation, the rusty patched bumblebee has declined roughly 87% in recent decades and was listed as endangered in 2017; threats include introduced plant pests, lack of cultural burning, evergreen trees encroaching on meadow habitat, and pathogens from managed bees. But Cheyenne says this bee is making a strong comeback in the Oneida reserve, with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service recently designating critical habitat nearby.

12:17 Cultural fire is not a government burn program with a different name
Both are controlled burns, but cultural fire is led by indigenous communities, with lower intensity, clearer intent, and timing determined by environmental cues like star positions; government and institutional burns are mostly about meeting area quotas. Indigenous community burns are motivated by ceremony or food sovereignty—a completely different logic from institutional burning's administrative goals.

23:42 Native American doctorate holders are less than one-third of one percent
According to 2024 article data, fewer than 2% of the U.S. population holds a doctorate; of that, only about one-third of one percent are Native Americans. Cheyenne says she rarely encountered scholars who looked like her or spoke like her growing up, which is why she once felt that getting a PhD ‘wasn't for someone like me’.

25:48 Dandelions tell the Tuscarora when their fish are spawning
Dandelions are a post-colonial introduction to North America, but their bloom period aligns with the spawning season of sturgeon culturally significant to the Tuscarora Nation and is still used as an important environmental signal. Similarly, Asian ladybugs were introduced for biological pest control and have crowded out native seven-spotted and nine-spotted ladybugs, yet they still eat aphids in the Three Sisters intercropping system and protect crops—so communities still acknowledge and respect the work they do.

37:22 The Haudenosaunee mosquito legend is about retaliation, not enmity
A Haudenosaunee story tells of two giant mosquitoes the size of trees that constantly attacked people paddling on the river; the people banded together to kill them, and when the giants fell, they scattered into countless tiny mosquitoes. Cheyenne says these small mosquitoes' existence today represents the mosquitoes retaliating for what the ancestors did—a ‘we struck first’ story, not one casting blood-sucking insects as pests to be eliminated.

54:07 The hardest part isn't fieldwork—it's defending why the work matters
Cheyenne says the most difficult part of her work isn't data analysis or writing, but constantly being asked ‘why is this important’ and ‘why should this shape policy’. She responds with one-on-one casual conversations, since a 12-minute academic presentation often can't convey the value of traditional ecological knowledge—the host notes with surprise that academia should be grateful for this knowledge rather than questioning it.

item.title: AI's 'agents' are misnamed: autonomy requires computational closure, not compute stacking
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-18-braininspired-ai-的-智能体-说法是误称-自主性要靠计算闭合-不是算力堆出来的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-18-braininspired-ai-的-智能体-说法是误称-自主性要靠计算闭合-不是算力堆出来的/
item.description: Determining autonomy is not about Turing completeness, but whether a system's internal loops can close on themselves—which is exactly where today's so-called AI agents fall short.
item.content:encoded:
Determining autonomy is not about Turing completeness, but whether a system's internal loops can close on themselves—which is exactly where today's so-called AI agents fall short.

This episode clarifies whether 'computation' actually applies to AI agents and brains; the tradeoff is working through high theoretical density.

20:14 Not all state changes and information transfer constitute computation
Not every information transfer or state change counts as computation. Nima developed a physical computation theory to provide a falsifiable definition, in contrast to casual neuroscience papers where 'that circuit computes X' often functions as an unjustified assertion.

32:45 Turing completeness does not guarantee autonomy
A French team demonstrated this with oil-droplet walkers: liquid droplets bounce on vibrating oil surfaces, with ripples feeding back to create chaotic trajectories with memory, erasure, and write primitives—Turing-complete, yet not autonomous. The closure comes from the experimenter flipping the wave phase externally, not from the system itself. This gap led Nima to develop the concept of computational closure: closure must emerge from within the system.

44:04 Calling AI systems 'agents' is a fundamental misnaming
Agency emerges from computational closure—when a system samples the environment, constructs an internal world model, and uses it to regulate its own behavior and state (like biological homeostatic setpoints). Today's AI systems called 'agents' lack this loop entirely. When they fail, it's described as the system 'going out of control,' but that gets the causality wrong—they didn't develop agency and rebel; humans simply didn't set the right boundaries.

1:06:00 Biology cannot afford backpropagation's weight-update machinery
Feedforward networks are straightforward to design and stack, but recurrent networks are another matter—Nima calls them 'neuroscience's holy grail.' While the brain must constantly change its operations, it cannot afford the rapid, large-scale weight updates that backpropagation requires. Nima breaks the problem into two basic building blocks: 'funnels' (systems with final states) and 'gears' (systems where states can reverse), using this framework to analyze what divisive normalization and winner-take-all circuits actually compute.

1:09:01 Two circuits combined can compute what each cannot alone
Divisive normalization in isolation produces only a limited set of output states, as does winner-take-all. Connect them in different directions—controlling which pushes which, where inputs flow—and the total state space expands dramatically. Even more striking: purely 'funnel'-based systems, when combined this way, suddenly produce 'gear'-like reversible behavior that neither component could achieve alone. Nima sees this as how evolution reuses modules, and suggests a path forward for designing recurrent systems based on mathematical prediction of combination effects, rather than relying on massive datasets and backpropagation.

1:18:21 Feedforward networks face mathematical barriers some problems cannot overcome
Nima is preparing a paper (already at the sixteenth revision) proving that certain physical problems are mathematically unsolvable by feedforward systems—they require recurrent architecture. He connects this to embodied knowledge: large language models can describe rain's temperature, paint it in Monet's style, write haiku about it, yet experience no rain. His dog never studied Galileo's physics but genuinely knows what rain is. This lived experience is what feedforward systems structurally cannot access; recurrence can.

1:22:24 Recurrent systems can learn without changing weights
Nima and collaborator Bahtash Babadi are completing a paper showing how a fully recurrent system can explicitly implement all the mathematics backpropagation performs—but without changing any weights. Learning happens in the system's recursive state rather than through weight updates. Nima is careful to note this is not a claim about how brains actually work, but rather a pointer toward where investigation should focus.

1:36:45 Not all brain activity is computation—some is information relay
When asked what fraction of brain processing is actual computation, Nima says he doesn't know. But he invokes David Deutsch's standard: good explanations must be difficult to arbitrarily patch when new phenomena appear. Using his current work on E. coli chemotaxis as an example, if he discovers that some component is merely information relay, he'll say so directly—rather than forcing the 'computation' label onto every corner of the system.

item.content:encoded:
Cai Wei believes model capability will eventually plateau with minimal provider differentiation; what truly separates winners is who controls more offline supply and whose security compliance work runs deeper.

Information density concentrates in the second half—business models, moat analysis and specific numbers are all there; the first half's product history can be skipped by anyone familiar with the AI industry.

28:21 Open-source projects proved models crossed the threshold for long-horizon task execution
Cai Wei notes that over this past Lunar New Year, an open-source agent project (called Open Cloud in the transcript) went viral. Though ordinary users spend two or three hours installing and configuring it—the experience is highly technical—it proved that models had crossed a threshold for long-horizon task execution: properly configured personas and skills can then orchestrate and execute numerous tasks automatically. This signal prompted nearly every major player to start personal agent projects after the new year. A hidden secondary theme is security, privacy and compliance. Muse also invested considerable time here, because for personal agents to be truly useful, users must willingly give up context to them—trust is a prerequisite, not a bonus feature.

37:31 Muse notifications feel like WeChat, not marketing spam
Cai Wei sees several personal agent products with similar feature lists but divergent experiences: the gap is primarily in what he calls 'boundary sense.' He observes that every Muse notification is carefully curated with sufficient information gain, creating a feedback loop where users think 'this message is worth opening'; but if you send morning and evening digests daily with low information density, users next time treat them as marketing messages and ignore them. This explains why personal agent products generally have higher retention—push has stopped being an engagement tool and become genuine feedback from the real world.

44:37 Three generations of AI products map to service industry worth 10 trillion yuan
Cai Wei maps the three generations of AI products unlocked by large models directly to market scale: Chatbots solve information retrieval, corresponding to the information sector at around 100 billion yuan; coding agents like Claude Code that complete tasks upend the software industry at the trillion-yuan scale; Personal Agents point to service industry restructuring—nutritionists, weight loss coaches, tutors and similar services now delivered by humans stand at 10 trillion yuan. He emphasizes the logic: estimate based on what currently solves this problem and how big that market is—the level of problems models solve maps directly to market scale.

49:38 Personal agents reshape supply, they don't just shift where scenarios happen
Cai Wei distinguishes two classes of innovation: mobile internet's transformation was fundamentally demand-side—smartphones unlocked location, letting users do what they couldn't before. Personal agents from this wave of large models are fundamentally supply-side restructuring: models can write answers on the fly, can recombine services scattered across different places into entirely new experiences. This distinction matters because a decade of O2O was actually laying the foundation for today's personal agents, letting them directly access offline supply that's now been moved online.

1:19:55 KPIs as targets inevitably distort execution
Cai Wei's product management philosophy: compress a direction into a specific metric—5 million DAU, 40% retention—and you necessarily lose massive amounts of high-dimensional information; teams instinctively pick the path easiest to hit the metric, but that's usually not the right path. He prefers explaining the product's principle and value clearly, letting the team understand the 'highest-level core,' so when external conditions shift the team can adjust without worrying whether work done against an old goal counts—especially in large companies where year-end performance reviews happen and constant KPI changes confuse everyone.

1:57:19 One error in ten steps means the whole sequence fails
Cai Wei explains with a mathematical intuition why personal agent experience remains far from ready: even if you improve single-step accuracy from 70% to 90%, a task split into ten steps means any failure breaks the whole chain; final success rate is one minus the product of all error rates. Even if each step has only a 3% error rate, multiply that over ten steps and overall success drops to 60-70%. This is why there's a canyon between 'can call tools' and 'calls them well and satisfies users'—leaderboard models only care about the former.

2:14:35 Intelligence will plateau; security and supply are the durable moat
Cai Wei breaks down personal agent competitive barriers by time horizon: in the short term, intelligence matters because model capability is still rapidly differentiating; but he judges intelligence will eventually plateau like the smartphone industry after iPhone 4—base models will all be much of a muchness, and what pulls ahead will be supply and trustworthy security. He sees this not as an indefinite hypothesis but as objective industry law, though we can't yet see when it will happen in the near term.

2:28:41 Personal agents compete on productivity replacement, not on traffic tolls
Cai Wei identifies two business models for personal agents: productivity logic, measuring whether the AI assistant's value creation exceeds its cost—if it creates 100 yuan monthly value and costs only 10 yuan, users have no reason not to use it, closer to hiring hourly labor; and internet-style traffic platform/toll logic, dependent on centralized traffic aggregation. He judges that if the personal agent ecosystem fragments, the first logic is likelier to hold because it doesn't depend on winner-take-all platform effects, just on individual unit value being high enough.

item.content:encoded:
Wang explains that unlike older technologies like databases, everyone has their own understanding of AI, so widespread adoption won't work through brainstorming. Enterprises should first build a closed-loop working model in one department, then use that as proof to convince the rest of the company to follow.

Practical case studies (Nano Banana, Manus selection), clear methodology, useful for anyone trying to understand how FDE actually lands enterprise AI.

3:02 Brain in a vat has no limbs
Wang's first reaction to seeing GPT-4 was: the problem of human thought is essentially solved—as an AI researcher working in applications, he immediately felt his past research was no longer necessary. But this new intelligence is just a "brain in a vat": no hands, no feet, only able to give answers in a chat window. Users have to manually copy generated code back to the editor. What FDE does is give this "brain" hands and feet, memory and scene-matching capability, turning it from a chat tool into an agent that can run in enterprise production systems.

10:05 Problem feedback doesn't leave the company
Wang says Google Cloud FDE's advantage isn't "stronger models" but a shorter debug loop: when FDE discovers capability boundaries on the customer site, they feed that directly back to internal product or model quality teams, then verify again after updates ship—internal communication within the company. If independent or third-party FDE can't solve a problem, they're looking at another company's tools; cross-organization communication is orders of magnitude slower. Third-party FDE's advantage is staying neutral between model vendors and helping customers compare options, but that's a tradeoff, not a capability advantage.

15:07 FDE sells model homes
Wang uses renovation as an analogy: a single house doesn't need a model home, just hire someone to renovate. But renovating an entire neighborhood means you must build a model home first—the model home may not have a toilet or mop, but it must have running water and electricity, meaning the demo doesn't need every feature, but the data pipeline must actually work in the real scenario and form a closed loop. His provocative take: enterprises can't push AI through brainstorming because unlike databases, where only one department understood the technology, everyone now has their own understanding of AI, making consensus impossible. The right approach is to make one department's model home beautiful and functional, then use that as proof to convince other departments to follow.

30:21 The boundary between R&D and PM melts first
Wang observed that before the Agent era, the line between his AI R&D team and PM team blurred first—developers started talking directly to LLMs to write project proposals and argue for algorithm value, work that used to be purely PM; PMs took R&D documents and asked LLMs for strategic direction, work that used to be purely R&D. He calls this phenomenon "FDE BP" (business partner): as vibe coding spreads, pure technical ability becomes secondary, what matters is whether you can reverse-engineer from customer business problems what kind of agent workflow is needed. This is making teams reconsider whether whiteboard coding belongs in hiring conversations anymore.

37:24 Don't ride the main channel, value is in the ripples
Wang describes a real case: a customer wanted to translate an entire ad image with pixel-level text from one language to another. He immediately objected because that sits squarely on the model's main channel—sure enough, two or three weeks later Google released Nano Banana and the whole custom system would have been obsolete. His conclusion: FDE should stand on the ship's sides looking for ripples, not at the bow. Needs on the main channel the model vendor will solve themselves soon. FDE's real job is finding the gaps to the sides and behind, the gaps the model still misses but customers genuinely need.

43:27 Mechanism can't buy trust
Wang says mechanism alone can't build trust—it can only help eliminate the last tiny bit of doubt. He uses Manus as an example: when multiple cloud vendors and model companies were pitching, what won was Google's FDE colleague solving concrete problems with enough initiative that trust slowly accumulated; only then could they discuss mechanisms like early model checkpoint access. He's blunt: agents still can't replace FDE because building trust face-to-face between people isn't automated yet.

48:32 Next wave explodes in knowledge workers
Wang's provocative take: the first AI wave already cashed out in programming; the next will blow up in knowledge work—sure, knowledge workers use fewer tokens per person than programmers, but feed the AI every meeting someone's attended and document they've written since joining the company, and tokens add up fast. He had a second ChatGPT moment using Gemini Agent for manager work: he doesn't have to tell AI which documents to look at or which meetings matter, just describe what he wants done and AI runs for a long time pulling context together. He calls this process "self-distillation" for knowledge workers and argues many enterprise AI failures aren't about AI itself, but about companies that skipped their digital transformation.

52:54 What took two months now finishes in one pass with agents
Wang contrasts his lived experience: using the old workflow (requirements document, architecture document, progress document all kept in sync with every change tracked) to build his wife's career coaching website—database design and full-stack deployment—took about two months of spare time. After Manus, he re-ran the same project without maintaining three documents or tracking changes, end-to-end, and got a basically functional page in one go. He sees agent evolution in layers: first round judges answer quality, second judges task completion, the next round will judge whether it matches how human brains process information at their natural pace—sometimes he wants one sentence, but the agent produces a five-minute read, and that mismatch hasn't been solved.
